question: Which writer owns creation of session-state.json, given that ai_router/session_state.py and the extension's utils/sessionState.ts both create it and the extension's copy is reached from a READ (readStatus)?
decision: The router's sanctioned writers own creation. The extension's read path stops writing: readStatus derives the same shape in memory (inferStateInMemory) and readSessionSets uses that derivation when the file is absent. ensureSessionStateFile is removed from the extension; synthesizeNotStartedState survives as an explicit-action writer only, and cancel/restore keep their own sanctioned writer. The rule: the extension writes session-state.json only on an explicit operator action, never on a read. Reversible cheaply — the removed write is one function and its call site, and the in-memory builder is the same code path the writer used.

options.option: Keep both writers and mirror the title logic, enforced by a parity test
options.consequence: The race survives: whichever writer reaches disk first still decides the ledger, and the next field added to the payload re-opens the same defect. Parity would prove agreement about titles, not about who writes.

options.option: Router owns creation; the extension's read derives in memory (chosen)
options.consequence: The race cannot happen — a scan produces no file at all. Removes a writer and an untracked-file side effect Set 099 S2 had already worked around with rawSessionSetStatus. Costs an in-memory branch in readSessionSets so spec-only sets keep their planned rows, and changes three tests that pinned the write side effect.

options.option: Extension owns creation; strip the Python lazy-synth
options.consequence: Inverts the constitution's state-mutation discipline (start_session / close_session are the sanctioned writers) and would leave consumer repos without a state file whenever the Explorer is not open.

question: A generic `Session N` title is sticky because title resolution puts the stored ledger first. 130 rows across the repo carry one, and most belong to CLOSED sets that will never get another boundary write. Where does the heal go, given spec decision 4 says this set does not move title resolution onto the read path?
decision: Heal in BOTH places through one shared pure rule (progress.heal_title, mirrored in progress.ts). The writer heals at every boundary write so the fix persists; the reader heals the display so closed sets — which get no further write — stop lying, with no migration script rewriting closed history. The reader's spec read is CONDITIONAL on needs_title_heal, so a healthy set costs no additional disk read, which is the measured constraint decision 4 was protecting. Reversible: the read-path heal is one guarded block per language.

options.option: Write-path heal only, honouring decision 4 literally
options.consequence: Fails this session's own Ends-with ('existing sets heal themselves'): ~130 rows in closed sets never get another boundary write and stay generic forever.

options.option: Write-path heal plus a conditional read-path heal (chosen)
options.consequence: Every set displays its real titles immediately, including closed ones. Costs one spec read per DRIFTED set per scan and none for healthy sets; the existing readSessionSets perf gate (p95 < 5000ms) is the falsifier.

options.option: A one-shot migration script that rewrites every drifted state file
options.consequence: Rewrites closed sets' records — the thing this repo treats as history — and the spec explicitly asks for healing WITHOUT a migration script. Also leaves the write-path bug in place for the next set.
